title: Why I’m Teaching Learning Before Anything Else
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A seventh-grade World Studies teacher explains why he opens the year with a ten-day Unit 0 called Learning How to Learn. His premise is that learning is not natural and is rarely fun, so students should be told the truth about effort, memory and retrieval before the content begins. The unit explains the cognitive science behind his daily routines (Do Now, retrieval, cold calling, mini-whiteboards) so that students understand why the class runs as it does rather than blaming themselves or him when it feels hard. He covers how memory works, retrieval practice, common learning myths, metacognition, and brain change through effort. The aim is a class culture of ownership and productive struggle from day one, rather than entertainment.
points: Learning is not natural or smooth, and telling students so up front resets expectations about effort and discomfort.
A short Unit 0 on memory, retrieval practice, myths and metacognition gives students the rationale behind classroom routines they would otherwise just endure.
Without that rationale, students who struggle conclude the problem is them or the teacher; understanding the process lets them treat learning as a skill they can improve.
The unit doubles as a tone-setting move for the start of the year: this class is about doing hard things, not being entertained.
quotes: Let me start with this: Learning isn’t natural. Our brains are not wired to learn biology, history, or algebra quickly and efficiently.
But real learning? The kind that sticks, the kind that changes your brain, that kind? It’s rarely fun. It’s work. It’s time consuming. It’s uncomfortable. It’s supposed to be.

Because my classroom runs on procedures and routines. Note-taking, Do Now, retrieval, cold calling, ruler readings, “no opt out” questioning, paired discussions, visible thinking routines, mini-whiteboards—you name it. But most students don’t know why we do any of this. They just go through the motions. And when it doesn’t work, they assume it’s a problem with them, or me.

We’re going to talk about brains. About memory. About why retrieval feels harder than rereading but works many times better. About how our memory actually works so we can make it work better. About what’s happening inside your head when you actually learn something. The science behind our procedures and routines.

I’m not here to entertain them. I’m here to teach them. That doesn’t mean class will be boring or miserable—but I won’t sugarcoat what learning takes. It will be challenging. It will be boring at times. And it won’t always feel good in the moment.

We don’t get better at basketball by watching others play. We don’t become great writers by only reading stories. And we don’t become better thinkers by coasting through lessons that are fun but forgettable. Learning takes work. That’s not a bug in the system—it’s the system.

More importantly, I hope they start seeing learning as something they can get better at. Not something you’re good at or not. Not something that just happens if the teacher is cool or the content is fun. But something you work at, improve at, and take ownership of.
